title.en: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'

text.en: Around the same time of the year, people across India celebrate harvest festivals, but each region has its own name and style: Pongal, Makar Sankranti, Lohri, Bihu. The foods, songs and clothes differ, yet the spirit is the same. In this chapter we see how India can be many and one at the same time.

India has over 1.4 billion people, about 18 percent of the world's population, so great diversity is not surprising. A survey counted 325 languages in 25 scripts. Many Indians are migrants in the sense of living far from their birthplace or original community, so even in your own region you meet people with different customs and traditions. The question is how to see and express unity in this variety, the Many in the One.
People in different regions eat different foods. Staple grains such as rice, wheat, millets and maize are the basic food for most Indians. Spices, vegetables and oils vary, and one vegetable can be cooked in many ways. Yet there is a common idea behind it: food is shared, enjoyed with family and offered to guests.
The sari is an unstitched piece of cloth that comes in hundreds of varieties, in cotton, silk and other materials. Some designs are woven in and others printed afterwards. A stone relief from Vaishali in Bihar, several centuries old BCE, shows a woman in a sari. There are many ways to wear it, which vary from region to region and community to community, but in the end it is a single dress.
Many festivals are celebrated across India at almost the same time, though with different names. Harvest festivals occur in January in many places, called Pongal, Makar Sankranti, Lohri and Magh Bihu. They connect people to the land, the seasons and farming, and are enjoyed by sharing sweets, songs and dances.
Indian literature is among the most abundant in the world. The Panchatantra, whose original Sanskrit text is at least 2,200 years old, has been adapted in almost every Indian language. The Ramayana and the Mahabharata, two Sanskrit epics which in the original might fill 7,000 pages, tell of heroes who fight to establish dharma. In the Ramayana, Rama with Lakshmana and Hanuman defeats Ravana, who had kidnapped Sita. There are countless folk versions. Most tribes of the northeast and Himalayan regions, including Kashmir, have their own version of one or both epics. As the text says, there is hardly a place in the country that the Pandavas did not visit according to folklore. This is another example of unity in diversity: one story, told in countless ways.

problem.en: Choose one custom from your home and find a similar one elsewhere in India.

text.en: Take Pongal: a harvest festival in Tamil Nadu.
Look for a harvest festival around the same time: Makar Sankranti, Lohri or Bihu.
The names, foods and songs differ but all thank the harvest.

prompt.en: How can India be both many and one?

requiredIdeas.en: Many languages, foods, dress and festivals.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking unity means everyone is the same.

points.en: India is extremely diverse in language, food, dress and festivals.
Common threads such as staple grains, the sari and harvest festivals run through the diversity.
The Panchatantra, Ramayana and Mahabharata have been told in countless languages.
Unity in diversity is a strength of India.
